clue.text: Children's author takes part in local cottage industry

indicators.note: the author's name takes up only part of the words local cottage, running across them

explanation.surface: A writer for children joins in a village cottage industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes part in' says the answer sits inside 'locAL COTTage'. Louisa May Alcott wrote Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisa May Alcott, of Little Women, is a celebrated American writer for young readers.

clue.text: Painting with new facet in object created

parts.note: painting is a form of art

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of facet are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A painting given a new facet within some created object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns FACET into EFACT, which follows ART.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is a man-made item, something crafted rather than natural.

clue.text: Trollope's came before Chesterfield

parts.note: Frances Trollope's 1841 novel is titled with a first name followed by the surname Chesterfield

explanation.surface: Something of Trollope's preceded the town or the earl of Chesterfield.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trollope is Frances, mother of Anthony: her novel is 'Charles Chesterfield, or the Adventures of a Youth of Genius'. With 21-down the entry also gives Charles Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename in the title of Frances Trollope's novel about the youth of genius is that of the hero, young Mr Chesterfield.

clue.text: I sanction new conductor

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of I sanction are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: An official approving a new conductor for the orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges the nine letters of I SANCTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Arturo Toscanini was the famous Italian orchestral maestro.

clue.text: He is often good at figures

definitions.text: He is often good at figures

parts.words: He is often good at figures
parts.note: figures read as carved statues rather than numbers

explanation.surface: Praise for someone who is good with numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figures' suggests arithmetic; here they are statues made by a carver.
explanation.definitionFit: A sculptor makes figures in stone, bronze or wood.

clue.text: Seasonal song from 2, 21

explanation.surface: A seasonal song taken from a writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 2, 21 is Charles Dickens, whose 1843 story bears this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A carol sung at Yuletide; also the title of Dickens's ghost story about Scrooge.

clue.text: Poem from early Richard le Gallienne

indicators.note: from says the poem is taken out of the run of letters in early Richard

explanation.surface: A poem by the young Richard Le Gallienne, the 1890s poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to the letters inside 'earLY RICHard'. Richard Le Gallienne was an English poet of the 1890s, which makes 'early' look like a period.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric is a short poem expressing personal feeling.

clue.text: Early ecologist wrote summer, winter and spring in Massachusetts

definitions.text: Early ecologist wrote summer, winter and spring in Massachusetts

parts.words: Early ecologist wrote summer, winter and spring in Massachusetts
parts.note: the writer of Walden chronicled the seasons by Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A pioneering naturalist recorded the passing seasons in New England.
explanation.walkthrough: Walden follows a year at the pond, its chapters including the seasons.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau recorded nature at Walden Pond and is often called a forerunner of the environmental movement.

clue.text: "These cates —— me, she but thought upon" (Pericles)

definitions.text: "These cates —— me, she but thought upon" (Pericles)

parts.words: "These cates —— me, she but thought upon" (Pericles)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: Pericles, Act 2 Scene 3, where the dainties will not go down while he thinks of Thaisa

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Pericles with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Cates are delicacies; Pericles cannot eat them, they repel him, when thinking of the princess.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to refuse or oppose, here food that will not be swallowed.

clue.text: He introduced a certain weekly literary periodical in which two of 2, 21's works appeared

definitions.text: He introduced a certain weekly literary periodical in which two of 2, 21's works appeared

parts.words: He introduced a certain weekly literary periodical in which two of 2, 21's works appeared
parts.note: the narrator who presents Dickens's weekly, the Clock, in which The Old Curiosity Shop and Barnaby Rudge were serialised

explanation.surface: Literary history: the figure who presented a weekly magazine of Dickens's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 2, 21 is Charles Dickens; his weekly of 1840-41 was named after this elderly narrator's clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Master Humphrey is the old man who opens Master Humphrey's Clock, the vehicle for two Dickens novels.

clue.text: "… a kind of garret-closet, accessible by a narrow — ascending from the lobby" (Robert Clarke, Life and Works of Robert Burns)

definitions.text: "… a kind of garret-closet, accessible by a narrow — ascending from the lobby" (Robert Clarke, Life and Works of Robert Burns)

parts.words: "… a kind of garret-closet, accessible by a narrow — ascending from the lobby" (Robert Clarke, Life and Works of Robert Burns)
parts.note: a quotation to complete with a word for steep steps through a hatch into a loft

explanation.surface: A description of the loft where Burns slept, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is a narrow ladder-like stair rising to a hatch, as in a Scottish cottage loft.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap-stair is a steep stair leading up through a trapdoor, the way into a garret.

clue.text: Origin of Wesker

explanation.surface: Where Arnold Wesker came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Wesker, English playwright, wrote the 1959 play of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Roots are a source or beginning; also the title of Arnold Wesker's play.

clue.text: Talk for thorough overhaul in traditional creative work

indicators.note: a thorough overhaul rebuilds something completely, so the letters of talk for are rearranged

explanation.surface: A discussion about a complete revamp of a traditional craft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thorough overhaul' rearranges the seven letters of TALK FOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Folk art is the craftwork of ordinary people in a traditional style.

clue.text: What William le Queux's FO stories ceased to be after publication

definitions.text: What William le Queux's FO stories ceased to be after publication

parts.words: What William le Queux's FO stories ceased to be after publication
parts.note: once printed, the contents were no longer hidden

explanation.surface: Spy stories about the Foreign Office lost something once printed.
explanation.walkthrough: FO is the British Foreign Office. Le Queux's book was 'Secrets of the Foreign Office', and anything published is no longer confidential.
explanation.definitionFit: Once in print, matters kept hidden are confidential no longer.

clue.text: Goddesses' foundations?

parts.note: foundations read as foundation garments: girdles such as that worn by Venus

explanation.surface: A query about what goddesses are built upon.
explanation.walkthrough: A foundation is also a corset or girdle; the cestus was the magic girdle of Aphrodite.
explanation.definitionFit: A cestus is a girdle in classical myth, notably Venus's; the plural is formed the Latin way.

clue.text: French notice German novelist

explanation.surface: A French notice about a German writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Erich Maria Remarque wrote All Quiet on the Western Front.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a remark or observation; also the author of All Quiet on the Western Front.

clue.text: Instrumental passage from Little Dorrit or Nell Gwyn

indicators.note: from says the passage is taken out of the letters of Little Dorrit or Nell Gwyn

explanation.surface: A piece of music taken from a Dickens novel or about Charles II's mistress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to 'dorRIT OR NELL'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ritornello is a recurring orchestral refrain; this is an English form of the word.

clue.text: She whom a gentleman may marrry (sounds like loose thinking)

definitions.text: She whom a gentleman may marrry (sounds like loose thinking)

parts.words: She whom a gentleman may marrry (sounds like loose thinking)
parts.note: Anita Loos wrote Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and its sequel But Gentlemen Marry ...; loose sounds like her surname

explanation.surface: A woman a gentleman might wed, though the idea seems a bit sloppy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose thinking' is Loos's thinking: Anita Loos followed Gentlemen Prefer Blondes with But Gentlemen Marry Brunettes. 'marrry' is printed with a misprint.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark-haired woman, the type Anita Loos said gentlemen end up wedding.

clue.text: What remains of Percy

explanation.surface: What is left of someone called Percy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Percy published 'Reliques of Ancient English Poetry' in 1765.
explanation.definitionFit: Relics, things left over, in an old spelling; also Bishop Percy's ballad collection.

clue.text: Lioness in winter?

parts.note: a nod to the play The Lion in Winter, about Henry II and his queen of Aquitaine

explanation.surface: A big cat facing the cold season.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Lion in Winter Henry II is the lion; his queen, Eleanor of Aquitaine, is his female match.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor of Aquitaine is the formidable queen opposite Henry II in The Lion in Winter.

clue.text: Royal family name of two of Trollope's civil servants (the third was Norman)

definitions.text: Royal family name of two of Trollope's civil servants (the third was Norman)

parts.words: Royal family name of two of Trollope's civil servants (the third was Norman)
parts.note: in The Three Clerks, Alaric and Charley share a surname that is an English royal house, and Harry is Norman

explanation.surface: Trollope's clerks are named after royal houses, one being Norman.
explanation.walkthrough: Trollope's The Three Clerks has Alaric and Charley, cousins, plus Harry Norman. Norman is also a royal house, which is the clue's play.
explanation.definitionFit: The dynasty of Henry VIII and Elizabeth I shares its name with two of Trollope's clerks.

clue.text: The devil of a writer

explanation.surface: A writer who is a real devil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What the dickens?' uses the word as a mild oath for the devil. With 2-down it gives Charles Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: An old euphemism for Satan, as in 'what the dickens'; also the Victorian novelist.

clue.text: Juliet was like a jewel in his ear, thought Romeo

definitions.text: Juliet was like a jewel in his ear, thought Romeo

parts.words: Juliet was like a jewel in his ear, thought Romeo
parts.note: Romeo says she hangs upon the cheek of night like a rich jewel in an African's ear

explanation.surface: Romeo compares Juliet to an earring.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and Juliet, Act 1 Scene 5: 'Like a rich jewel in an Ethiop's ear'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for an Ethiopian or African, used in Romeo's simile.

clue.text: Arthur C. Clarke's range was so profound!

definitions.text: Arthur C. Clarke's range was so profound!

parts.words: Arthur C. Clarke's range was so profound!
parts.note: Range also suggests the scope of his work

explanation.surface: Admiring how wide and deep Arthur C. Clarke's work was.
explanation.walkthrough: Clarke's 1957 novel is The Deep Range; dropping 'Range' leaves a phrase meaning the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The deep' is a poetic name for the sea, the setting of Clarke's novel.

clue.text: Lady Snow drew attention to one of judgment

definitions.text: Lady Snow drew attention to one of judgment

parts.words: Lady Snow drew attention to one of judgment
parts.note: Pamela Hansford Johnson, wife of C. P. Snow

explanation.surface: A titled lady pointing out a misjudgment.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Snow is the novelist Pamela Hansford Johnson, who married C. P. Snow; her 1962 novel is An Error of Judgement.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake, as in her title 'An Error of Judgement'.

clue.text: Dinesen title, in a word

parts.note: Karen Blixen wrote Out of Africa; one adjective means coming from that continent

explanation.surface: Summing up a Karen Blixen book in one word.
explanation.walkthrough: Isak Dinesen (Karen Blixen) wrote 'Out of Africa'; something out of that continent is described by this single word.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming from the continent in Blixen's title, compressed into one adjective.

clue.text: Room for Merrill

parts.note: James Merrill's poetry collection The ___ Room, 1988

explanation.surface: Making space for someone called Merrill.
explanation.walkthrough: The American poet James Merrill published 'The Inner Room'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inner room is one deep within a house, the title of Merrill's book.

clue.text: Rumoured war hero's bear species named for him

definitions.text: Rumoured war hero's bear species named for him

parts.words: Rumoured war hero's bear species named for him
parts.note: the teddy bear is said to be named after Theodore, the Rough Rider of San Juan Hill

explanation.surface: A war hero who reportedly had a kind of bear named after him.
explanation.walkthrough: Theodore Roosevelt led the Rough Riders in the Spanish-American War; the toy teddy bear is said to be named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Teddy Roosevelt, US president and Rough Rider, gave his nickname to the teddy bear.

clue.text: How artist describes the beams that are left

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
beams of light are rays

explanation.surface: An artist depicting light that remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like 'remaining' in the surface but means port, the nautical left.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist depicts or represents a subject in a picture.

clue.text: President's residence in cathedral diocese

parts.note: Ely, in Cambridgeshire, is a famous English cathedral city
a see is a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: Where a president lives within a cathedral's diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY is an English cathedral city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Élysée Palace in Paris is the official home of the French head of state.
